title: Lesson 51: Agent Identity: OAuth, Service Accounts, and Scoped Permissions
description: An agent is a machine actor, and a machine actor needs a machine identity: credentials it can present to an API, a scope limited to the least it needs to do, and a way to be rotated and revoked when it is no longer trusted. The authorization code grant lets an agent act on a specific user's behalf without ever seeing the user's password, while the client credentials grant lets it act on its own behalf using its own credentials. A service account gives a long-running agent a durable non-human identity with its own permissions, and OAuth scopes express least privilege by limiting what a token may do.

questions.question: An agent must act on behalf of a specific user, with that user's approval, without ever seeing the password. Which flow fits?
options: The client credentials grant, because the agent acts with its own identity
The authorization code grant, because the user approves the access
A shared human account, because it already has the user's permissions
A long-lived static API key stored in the agent's configuration
questions.explanation: Delegated work uses the authorization code grant: the user authenticates and approves at the authorization server, and the password never reaches the agent. The client credentials grant is for an agent acting on its own behalf with no user in the loop.

questions.question: Why give a long-running agent its own service account instead of borrowing a human's credentials?
options: A service account is a non-human identity with its own credentials
A service account inherits the full permissions of whoever created it
A service account never needs its credentials rotated or stored securely
A service account lets the agent skip authentication to the resource server
questions.explanation: A service account is a separate principal with its own credentials and permissions, so the agent does not borrow a human's access or share a human's secret. It can be scoped, rotated, and revoked without touching any person.

questions.question: What limits the damage if an agent's token or key leaks?
options: The model's system prompt, which tells it to refuse harmful calls
The provider, which detects and blocks unauthorized requests
The scopes granted to the token, which the server enforces
The agent's logs, which record what the attacker does
questions.explanation: Scopes express least privilege: the token can do only what it was granted, and the resource server enforces that on each request. The narrower the scope, the smaller the blast radius when credentials leak.
